question.problem: Find and categorize all local the extrema of the function $f(x,y)=xy-4x-4y-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ and determine which of the following statements is true.
question.worked_solution:
The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-4x-4y-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-4x-4y-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}y-4-2x & x-4-2y\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y-4-2x=0 \\ x-4-2y=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get

$$
y-4-2x=0\,⟹\,y=2x+4
$$

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-4-2(2x+4) & =0 \\ -3x-12 & =0 \\ x & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting these values into $y=2x+4,$ we obtain

$$
x=-4\,⟹\,y=2(-4)+4=-4.
$$

Hence, $(-4,-4)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-4-2x)=-2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-4-2y)=1 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-4-2)=1\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-4-2y)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(-4,-4),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-4,-4)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(-4,-4),$ we get

$$
H(-4,-4)=det({f}^{″}(-4,-4))=(-2)^{2}-{1}^{2}=3>0.
$$

Finally, notice that 

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-4,-4)=({f}^{″}(-4,-4))_{11}=-2<0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(-4,-4).$
